articles.title_orig: Thousands Expected to Protest in France on Halloween: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Thousands Expected to Protest in France on Halloween: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Mark Landler and Ségolène Le Stradic
Hundreds of thousands of protesters were on the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, a now-weekly expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police, and kept the country on edge.
Adding to those fears: Halloween, which also falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.
In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired rounds of tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration in the city, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people had demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.
Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.
There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.
The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.
The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.
“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.
Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather in spite of the ban will lead to arrests, he said.
Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration in which public order is disrupted.
Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people and inciting them to violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›
Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often end up in clashes with far-left groups.
Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›
Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.
Among the protesters in the unauthorized demonstration were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom were wearing white T-shirts indicating that they were “street medics,” or those able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she came to demonstrate because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school. Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he was prompted to join when his little brother told him about getting tear-gassed and almost hit by a stun grenade at a protest earlier this month. “The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.” On Saturday, the pair said they saw one person who had been injured in the head, but aid arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said. (Ségo)
I can hear loud bangs at the end of the demonstration route and I can see many people running backward, as well as tear gas in the distance. Some protesters are throwing mortar-like fireworks.
The mood at the Paris protest has definitely changed. Though I can still hear some protesters singing, the protest has turned violent.
Police officers are now blocking many of the roads in the neighborhood at the end of the demonstration route. I saw a young woman surrounded by medics — she was bleeding from the face. I saw flames at the end of one avenue. I also saw police officers charge toward the crowd. Some residents are trying to make their way back home quickly, covering their faces to avoid tear gas.
Tensions in Paris continue to rise. Police are skirmishing with 200 to 300 rioters who have refused to disperse at the end of a rally. The Paris police said the rioters threw Molotov cocktails and fireworks at officers. A car was set afire.
Tensions are now flaring between protesters and the police in Paris. Police are firing rounds of tear gas at people, who are refusing to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday.
The Interior Ministry estimated that 320,000 people took part in protests across the country today. That is somewhat fewer than last week (410,000) and the week before (550,000).
The demonstration in Paris remains peaceful, even festive. But police and protesters have clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes. Tear gas and water cannons have been deployed as the police try to disperse crowds. Violence typically breaks out at the end of these rallies, when people refuse to leave the scene.
I am walking along the authorized route for the demonstration in Paris. For the most part, the mood has been festive. Someone even dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers from the crowd.
After, I watched a half-dozen protesters dressed in black and wearing masks push trash bins in the middle of the crowd. One was already burning as they made their way, and they set the second on fire not far from where a police unit was stationed. Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, causing a small clash with the ones wearing in black. “That’s no way to protest,” one of the demonstrators who put out the fire said.
The protest in Paris has a joyous and playful atmosphere. Brass bands are playing music, and many protesters have come dressed in Halloween costumes. Many said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17 when riots spilled out of marches across France, leading to destruction and looting.
“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who came dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”
Literature student Arthur Fleury, 20, arrived as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wore a mask of the far-right politician Marine Le Pen. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”
Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggest crowds are smaller today than the past two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. That compares to 37,000 people last week at that time and 67,000 on Oct. 17. These numbers can be expected to grow as the day progresses. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by this time last Saturda

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran's supreme leader warns U.S., Israel against new attacks
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran's supreme leader warns U.S., Israel against new attacks
articles.content_orig:
Iran has claimed another ship transiting the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz hit a mine and is on fire, according to semi-official Fars News Agency.
"This afternoon, a violating oil tanker that, disregarding warnings, was transiting in the prohibited and unsafe area in the east of the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire after striking sea mines," the country's navy said, according to Fars News Agency.
The news could not immediately be verified.
Iran has claimed nearly 10 ships have hit mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, specifically along the Omani coastline. That shipping lane is favored by the U.S. and is considered prohibited by Iran. Of the 81 attacks on ships in the strait since July 6, 59 of them have been on the southern route, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre.
President Trump has not made a decision about new strikes on Iran amid stalled peace talks, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday.
"We can achieve military objectives if we seek to. He hasn't made a decision. I have no announcement in that regard with you today, and nor do we take any of it lightly," Rubio said at a G20 press conference in Atlanta.
"If we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it and we have everything we need to be successful," Rubio added. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
He also would not characterize whether progress has been made in the last few days and said there is no timeframe on talks between the U.S. and Iran through its mediators.
Rubio continued to echo many of the things Mr. Trump has said in recent weeks and months. The United States' main objective is to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, and Rubio emphasized the threat to the rest of the world if they do.
"The Iranian regime is basically arguing is, 'Unless we get what we want, not only will we blow up ships, but we will destroy the energy infrastructure of our neighbors and the entire region.' Just think about that," Rubio said. "Because I think that we skip over that like that's some sort of normal behavior. That's not normal behavior, but we are there to help protect against it."
Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage, according to an Associated Press analysis .
The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The AP found that Iran initially focused its attacks on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, clearing the way for further strikes on warehouses, troop housing and more.
The damage has significantly reshaped the American foothold in the Middle East, with two regional officials saying the U.S. has moved many of its assets out of the Persian Gulf. That includes aircraft, air defense systems, communications systems and other equipment crucial to base operations, one of those officials said.
Most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, while U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted, the analysis of satellite imagery shows.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.
Camp Buehring, also in Kuwait, faced even heavier losses. While Iranian attacks made most of its hangars inoperable, gathering places for troops sustained much more damage because the base had limited aircraft. Its gym was destroyed in March and a store for troops to buy products on the base was hit in late July.
Iran's top diplomat on Saturday said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States despite growing concerns over a return to war.
"Currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials, and any speculation to the contrary is merely media assumption," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
"We see no need to meet with the Americans at present, our conditions are clear, and the mediators continue their consultations regarding them," Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
Qatari and Pakistani mediators met in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday, where an Iranian delegation was present. Iranian officials, through the Qatari mediators, received an outline for a peace deal from the U.S. last weekend, spearheaded by Vice President JD Vance.
"The American side's attempt to open the door to broader dialogue and understanding is considered a positive step, and if Washington's goal from Vance's message is to stir up differences, it will be a new mistake added to its previous errors," Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said on Saturday the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement to end the crisis with Iran.
"If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.
Concerns are rising about a return to all-out war, especially after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S. President Trump has opined during recent rallies that he could quickly bring the war to an end through military action.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
"We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere," he said.
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, on Saturday warned the United States against launching fresh attacks, amid weeks of heightened tensions and repeated threats.
"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his Telegram channel.
The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.
Khamenei has not been seen publicly since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's killing in U.S.-Israeli strikes at the start of the war in February.
According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response."
Saudi air defences intercepted a drone in the Riyadh region on Saturday, according to the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone in the Riyadh region," Turki al-Malki wrote on X, adding that "debris from the interception fell without causing injuries." Malki did not say who launched the drone.
In recent weeks, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that forced its closure for two weeks and the cancellation of flagship events.
On Friday, Malki said the Houthis had targeted the Medina region, home to Islam's second holiest city, but the group later denied the claim.

articles.title_orig: Xona Is in Orbit. Its CEO Says U.S. GPS Backup Leans on China.
articles.title_zh: Xona Is in Orbit. Its CEO Says U.S. GPS Backup Leans on China.
articles.content_orig:
By Nick David, Editorial Lead, SatNews
Xona Space Systems put its first six commercial navigation satellites in orbit last week. On Thursday, its CEO laid out why the U.S. needs them: the backup most commercial users rely on today comes from China.
“We actually just launched our first six satellites last week that are going to start providing commercial service early next year,” Xona co-founder and CEO Brian Manning said on the MilSat Symposium panel “GPS Under Attack: Jamming, Spoofing, and the PNT Fight” at Silicon Valley Space Week, moderated by Ahsun Murad of Optimal Satcom. The Pulsar satellites flew Oct. 20 on SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 rideshare, and Xona has said beta service begins in early 2027. The company closed a $250 million Series D two days after launch.
Manning said the problem is already showing up in drones built by the hundreds of thousands. Drone companies on the military side “are cutting the cable on the GPS chip because they don’t trust it,” he said. “It’s actually worse to have bad location than no location.” Jamming can be worked around with inertial sensors, but bad location “means you’re going to hit your own troops.”
Those builders don’t have access to M-code or other secure signals, Manning said, while faking GPS signals takes about as much skill as “typing the Google.”
Commercial users trying to make positioning more resilient mostly move to multi-constellation receivers, Manning said, and the newest constellation beyond GPS is China’s. U.S. industries from critical infrastructure timing to agriculture to logistics now integrate Chinese signals alongside GPS, “a vulnerability that has been ingrained into pretty much every single aspect of U.S. critical infrastructure,” he said.
Receiver makers can’t simply drop those signals and stay competitive globally, he acknowledged. “But right now relying on Chinese, Russian, et cetera, signals to get resilience does not put the U.S., I don’t think, in a very strong position.”
Col. Jon Strizzi, director of Space Systems Command’s Space Systems Integration Office, gave the Space Force’s GPS update. He said 14 GPS IIIF satellites, the next block, are on contract, with five moving through assembly, integration and test and first deliveries expected in mid-2027.
The panel also included Jeff Janicik, founder and chairman of Innoflight; Monali Jain, founder and CEO of AutonomousLabs.Space; and Sumant Sharma, co-founder and CEO of EraDrive.
Xona’s pitch is that commercial signals from low Earth orbit, roughly 20 times closer to Earth than GPS, can add the precision, power and protection that today’s receivers lack while plugging into the billions of GPS devices already in use.
A storyteller at heart, Nick David covers space policy, satellite markets, defense, and the technologies reshaping how humanity operates beyond Earth. With a background in creative direction, brand strategy, and editorial storytelling, he brings a modern lens to complex subjects and a relentless curiosity about what comes next.
Satnews is a leading provider of satellite news, events, publications, research and other satellite industry information in both commercial and military enterprises worldwide.

articles.title_orig: American chip billionaire Jensen Huang's Nvidia defends his meetings with suspected Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: American chip billionaire Jensen Huang's Nvidia defends his meetings with suspected Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia says billionaire CEO Jensen Huang did nothing unusual in meeting a Chinese executive whom U.S. intelligence officials concluded was gathering information for Beijing.
Nvidia Corp. has defended its billionaire chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, after a report that U.S. intelligence officials concluded a Chinese businesswoman who built a close relationship with him was gathering information for Beijing, and that President Donald Trump was told about it roughly a year ago but did not act.
The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese national and a former senior executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that buys Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips and rents out computing power, including to Chinese companies. She has not been charged with any crime, and neither has Megaspeed. U.S. officials did not believe Jensen Huang knew she was collecting information for China, according to people familiar with the classified intelligence. No one has accused him of wrongdoing.
Nvidia said the contacts were routine. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected," Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said. "Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The company said customers such as Megaspeed receive ordinary business information, not trade secrets or anything tied to national security, and that it was confident the government would tell it if it believed someone was a threat to American industry.
Huang, 63, called Nvidia's business with Megaspeed normal on Oct. 29 and said the company had checked how the cloud provider used its chips. "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one," he said. He added that Alice Huang no longer works at Megaspeed.
U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang turned up her contacts with Jensen Huang and led officials to conclude she was passing information to Beijing, according to people familiar with the intelligence. Officials worried she could gain access to sensitive Nvidia technology or insight into Trump's thinking on chip exports to China. The two were photographed together at a bar in Taipei in June 2024 and were seen at a business dinner in May 2025.
Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago. The administration took no action, and Jensen Huang never received a defensive briefing, the warning U.S. agencies sometimes give Americans who are being targeted by a foreign intelligence service. The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency declined to comment.
Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment. Megaspeed said it takes the matter seriously, has hired outside lawyers to run an internal investigation and has told U.S. authorities it will cooperate. China rejected the report. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called it "baseless and purely slanderous," and the Chinese Embassy in Washington described U.S. accusations as "groundless smears and slanders."
Megaspeed under investigation
The U.S. began looking at Megaspeed in late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visiting its data center in Malaysia found Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes. Investigators suspected some of its chips were reaching China in breach of U.S. export rules, which bar the sale of Nvidia's most advanced processors there. A Malaysian sister company of Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records. Singapore authorities questioned Alice Huang in 2025 and released her.
Senator Tom Cotton asked the Commerce Department in October 2025 to investigate Megaspeed, and the Justice Department took over the case this year. Nvidia said earlier claims that Megaspeed helped Chinese buyers evade U.S. restrictions "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year." Megaspeed remains a listed Nvidia cloud partner.
The report lands at a sensitive time for Huang, who has become one of Trump's closest business allies. He persuaded the president to allow some chip sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government taking a share of the revenue, and he was a guest at the White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. Trump personally owns Nvidia shares.
Born in Taiwan, Huang moved to the U.S. as a child and co-founded Nvidia in 1993. He has run the company ever since, turning a maker of graphics cards for video games into the dominant supplier of the chips used to build AI systems. His stake in Nvidia has made him one of the richest people in the world.

articles.title_orig: Poland's president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country's top court
articles.title_zh: Poland's president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country's top court
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
WARSAW — Hundreds of anti-government protesters rallied overnight outside Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal to denounce the suspension of its president, a move they blame on the country’s pro-European government.
Police said they detained three protesters after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Saturday, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal amid the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building.
Nawrocki said that a “breach of Poland’s constitutional order” had taken place and invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution.
“Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to Nawrocki, told the Associated Press.
The Tusk government said it acted to restore the independence of the judiciary.
The government is a broad coalition made up of the prime minister’s centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Third Way and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Third Way and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday. Tusk did not attend.
The president’s camp is hoping the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority.
The protests over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal are likely to sharpen the battle between Tusk’s pro-European government and its opponents, chiefly the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice, or PiS.
Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country from 2015 to 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Changes introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland.
Tusk’s government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki.
On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal’s website announced the suspension of court president Bogdan Swieczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader and former Prime Minister Jaroslaw Kaczynski and other far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building.
The government says Swieczkowski repeatedly broke the law and jeopardized the tribunal’s work. Swieczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking.
Politicians from PiS have criticized Swieczkowski’s suspension.
“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X late Friday. “That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless.”
Ciobanu writes for the Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.title_zh: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.content_orig:
We have Muse Charm at home.
We have Muse Charm at home.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home . It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio , but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C . Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well , Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address . (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

articles.title_orig: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.title_zh: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.content_orig:
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Shares of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) rose 8.9% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 0.3%. The gain came a day after Chipotle reported its third-quarter results on October 28. Revenue came in above estimates, while adjusted earnings per share fell below them. Four of the chain’s five peers also posted smaller gains during that session. What in Chipotle’s results did news reports link to the rise?
Chipotle Topped Sales Estimates As Transactions Rose
Chipotle’s third-quarter revenue reached $3,293 million, a little above the $3,287 million analysts expected. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.27, below the $0.29 estimate. The company released its results after the market closed on Wednesday. News reports linked Thursday’s rise to same-store sales that topped estimates, as well as to the chain’s push to bring customer traffic back .
During the October 28 call, management said same-store sales increased 2.1% in the quarter and transactions rose 0.8%. It added that Pollo Asado’s return on August 31 brought in extra transactions, while Chili Lime Chips, launched the same day, got more guests to add chips.
Fresh products give buyers a reason to return; an unchanged lineup can stall. Consider Tesla, which got 98% of last quarter’s deliveries from the Model 3 and Model Y and saw deliveries fall two years in a row. Read Trefis Big Story : How Tesla Blundered .
The industry saw a pullback in the first part of October, management said, but Chipotle’s transactions have since turned positive again. Management expects fourth-quarter same-store sales to rise around 2% overall, with the growth rate reaching 3% to 4% by the end of the quarter as smoked brisket returns to the menu in November.
Margins slipped in the quarter. Management put the company’s restaurant-level margin, its own adjusted measure, at 23.3%. That figure is down 120 basis points from a year earlier.
Did Chipotle Rise With Its Restaurant Peers?
Most of Chipotle’s peers also rose, though by much less. Four of the five companies on the Trefis peer list gained during the session, leaving Restaurant Brands International as the only decline. Texas Roadhouse posted the largest advance among them at 4.7%. The consumer discretionary sector fund, XLY, rose 0.8% on a day the S&P 500 fell. Chipotle rose almost twice as much as Texas Roadhouse, so a large part of its gain was its own rather than the group’s.
Where Does Chipotle Stock Stand After The Jump?
A rise this large is rare for Chipotle. One session in the prior 365 days saw a rise at least as big. After the jump, the stock was still down 22.3% over the twelve months to October 29, compared with a 13.3% gain for the S&P 500.
Much of that fall occurred in the last three months. The shares lost 16.0% from July 31 to October 29, while the S&P 500 rose 3.3%. Chipotle closed the session at $31.28. That price sits above the stock’s 52-week closing low of $27.52 set on October 23, 2026, and remains well below the closing high of $40.87 reached on January 23, 2026.
Chipotle is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in February 2027. Same-store sales growth is the figure to watch in that report.
Sitting On A Big Gain In Chipotle Mexican Grill?

articles.title_orig: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.title_zh: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.content_orig:
Experts now say passkeys like biometrics and face ID are now the best way to protect our digital lives.
You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device.
Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself.
Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money
In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay.
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES
Cybercriminals can access online accounts without stealing passwords by hijacking login sessions, exploiting security approvals or abusing connected apps. (Photo by Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step.
How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session.
Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password-reset message you did not request.
How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone.
ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU?
Stolen session cookies and malicious browser extensions can give hackers access to sensitive accounts, even when strong passwords are in place. (Photo by Britta Pedersen/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code.
How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals.
An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual.
How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure.
Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password. This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions.
How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features.
Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process.
How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current.

articles.title_orig: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.title_zh: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Big Tech's brutal week had one clear epicenter. Alphabet ( GOOGL ) lost $468 billion in market value this week, more than SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia combined.
That was the Google parent's worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $552 billion in the week of Jan. 27, 2025, when China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet's previous worst was about $386 billion in the week ended June 26.
Most of the damage came Thursday, when Alphabet lost $475 billion in a single session after its third quarter results . Friday's slide wiped out the gains the stock had made earlier in the week.
October was even worse. Alphabet shed about $758 billion in market value this month, the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company. Only SpaceX ( SPCX ) has lost more, about $822 billion in July. Alphabet's October loss is nearly double its previous worst month, about $420 billion in February 2025.
In percentage terms, the stock fell nearly 19% in October, its worst month since it went public in 2004. Its previous worst was an 18.5% drop in November 2008. For the week, it fell nearly 13%, its worst since August 2011.
The selloff has left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade .
SpaceX, Intel ( INTC ) and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week. Intel fell as much as 30% Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades . Amazon ( AMZN ) shed about $80 billion for the week after reporting results Thursday. Some software names fell harder in percentage terms, with ServiceNow ( NOW ) and Fortinet ( FTNT ) down roughly 25% to 34%.
Not all of that money left the market. Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Tesla ( TSLA ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) added more than $300 billion in combined value, even as the Magnificent 7 stumbled .
UBS's chief investment office argued against heading for the exits. "Further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote Friday. "We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech."
The close settled it. October goes down as Alphabet's worst month since its IPO, in dollars and in percentage terms. The stock finished the week about $7 above the roughly $273 level it would have needed to take Nvidia's weekly record.

articles.title_orig: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.title_zh: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.content_orig:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said Saturday that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Khamenei made the remark on X after meeting with senior commanders of the Iranian military.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he wrote.
"The military target database must be updated comprehensively to ensure that all kinds of physical and non-physical assets" of the U.S. and Israel "are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," Khamenei also said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump "hasn't made a decision" whether or not to resume strikes on Iran.
Rubio, speaking at the G20 meeting in Atlanta, said Trump prefers to solve the conflict diplomatically.
"This is also a country and a regime that is at the center of all the instability in the Middle East," Rubio said earlier. "In Lebanon there is instability because they support Hezbollah. In Saudi Arabia they are under attack because Iran supports the Houthis. In Iraq, is a country that is feeling challenged because Iranian-backed militias are challenging the state there. So anywhere you turn what you find is some Iranian proxy that's undermining the peace and stability of the Middle East. That is a fundamental threat that we have to confront, on top of the fact that they want nuclear weapons."
"This is a regime that has massacred its own people," he added. "You could only imagine what it would do to others if it possessed weapons of mass destruction, which will never be allowed to happen as long as President Trump is in the White House."
Strikes launched by Iran against more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East have resulted in billions of dollars of equipment damage, according to The Associated Press.
The news agency cited its analysis on satellite imagery from multiple providers and said it spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit.
The AP reported that through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with American equipment. Many of the attacks focused on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, the AP added.
It said most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, but U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to the AP.
This satellite image taken over Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait on July 24, 2026, shows the result of numerous strikes on this section of the bas. (Airbus DS 2026 via AP)
Al Dhafra Air Base, about 20 miles south of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, was hit frequently early in the war, a regional military official with direct knowledge of the damage told the AP. The official noted damage to infrastructure like aircraft hangars and other installations as well as to equipment such as an early-warning radar system and surveillance drones.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the AP that U.S. “forces and bases are well protected and America’s military is stronger than ever.”
“Our service members in CENTCOM have everything they need to continue their historic success ensuring Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon,” he added.
The Associated Press contributed to this post.
Major Gen. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the armed forces of Iran, insisted Saturday that the country's military would respond quickly to any attacks.
"Whenever signs of hostile enemy action are confirmed, the armed forces will not wait for the start of his action in choosing the time and manner of response," he wrote on X.
"With all informational capacity, we monitor the enemy's movements and preparations and update the target bank," Abdollahi added.
He made the remark in response to a call from Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to confront any threat "with an immediate, effective, and unrestricted geographical response."
Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Tehran currently has no plans to meet with U.S. officials for talks aimed at ending the war.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at present. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” Araghchi reportedly said, adding, “What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation.”
The remarks come after an official told Reuters Saturday that Iranian negotiators are meeting with Qatari mediators in Doha.
The Qatari team has been in frequent contact with the U.S. during the discussions, Reuters cited an official briefed on the negotiations as saying.
Negotiators from Iran are in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday for talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the U.S.-Iran war, according to Reuters.
The Qatari team has been in frequent contact with the U.S. during the discussions, it cited an official briefed on the negotiations as saying.
The official added that Saturday's talks come after more than 12 hours of negotiations in Tehran, Iran, on Friday.
The U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran on Feb. 28.
Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs Waleed ElKhereiji said Saturday that people "want to bring peace back to the region" during the U.S.-Iran war.
ElKhereiji made the remark during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain, where he added that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the conflict with Iran.
“If you look at… the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear," ElKhereiji said, according to The Associated Press. "People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region."
The Associated Press contributed to this post.
U.S. Central Command released a new image Saturday of a F/A-18 Super Hornet jet on the flight deck of the USS George H.W. Bush during nighttime operations.
The aircraft carrier has operated in the Middle East in support of the U.S. military's blockade on Iranian ports.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said this week that "since day one, America's sons and daughters, serving in the Middle East, have shown relentless commitment, dedication, and courage.
"It's been the honor of a lifetime to serve alongside them and recognize them for the tremendous accomplishments on behalf of the nation," Cooper added. "As their commander, I could not be prouder, and I know that the families, friends, loved ones, and the American people back home share in this pride."
The Trump administration warned Iran that there "will be consequences" if Tehran continues its malign activities amid growing concern over a potential new round of U.S.-Iran hostilities after the midterm elections.
With just days until the 2026 elections and with war raging on in the Middle East, foreign ministers from the world's largest economies gathered in Atlanta, Georgia ahead of the G20 leaders meeting in December.
"The Iranian regime has had a choice... to either pursue the path towards normalcy, towards prosperity for their people, the path towards diplomacy. Or they can continue their malign activities, but there will be consequences for that, and we've seen the president taking concrete action," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.title_zh: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.
In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.
"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

articles.title_orig: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
articles.title_zh: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
articles.content_orig:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia
The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.
The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia .
The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, which had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, made an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.
For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.
It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.
The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.
At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.
On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.
“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”
The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.
“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”
Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.
One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube , including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.
“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.
Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.
The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.
“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.
Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.
The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.
Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.
“I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”
Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”
Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”
While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.
“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.
Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Gadi Eisenkot is the bereaved general trying to outmaneuver Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Gadi Eisenkot is the bereaved general trying to outmaneuver Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections .
Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
So how could a new government be formed?
Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible.
Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls.
Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that.
On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle.
Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office.
Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged.
Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind.
Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers.
But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar.
While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament.
Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first.
Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed.
If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out.
After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition.
If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election.
The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed.
A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.

articles.title_orig: Apple Reveals New iPad Mini's Battery Capacity
articles.title_zh: Apple Reveals New iPad Mini's Battery Capacity
articles.content_orig:
Apple has published an EU energy label for the iPad mini 8 that reveals the device has a battery capacity of 4,900 mAh, which is slightly lower than the 5,034 mAh capacity of the previous model's battery.
Apple's website lists identical battery life estimates for both models, so it appears that the improved power efficiency of the A20 Pro chip in the new iPad mini helps to offset its slightly smaller battery. The new model is also equipped with an OLED display, which can be more power efficient than an LCD when displaying darker content, as there is no backlight and individual pixels turn off completely for the color black.
For those who prefer watt-hour figures, Apple's tech specs show the new iPad mini has an 18.9 Wh battery, down from 19.3 Wh for the previous model.
The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch OLED display, a new Acoustic Display audio system instead of speaker holes, Wi-Fi 7 support, a 15% thinner and lighter design compared to the previous model, and more . The device is available to pre-order now and launches on Friday, November 6, with U.S. pricing starting at $699.
