articles.title_orig: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections
articles.title_zh: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections
articles.content_orig:
Akhtar is a foreign correspondent for The Telegraph based in London
Iran is preparing to disrupt the US midterm elections after attempting to interfere in Israel’s vote this week , The Telegraph can reveal.
Several Iranian officials said Tehran viewed the near-simultaneous elections of its two biggest enemies as a rare opportunity to exploit vulnerabilities in their democratic systems.
“We have been looking into ways to recruit agents in both the American and Israeli regimes’ election processes,” one official said. He added that “powerful cyber groups have also been established to hack their election systems”.
Another official framed the effort as the natural extension of a war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
“War does not just mean missiles and guns when we are under their blockade,” he said.
“It also means we are prepared to disrupt their elections, their banking, their travel and all their ordinary systems. We are not in favour of any candidate anywhere, but we would like to see a divided America and a divided Israel .”
That, in the end, is Tehran’s prize.
Eight months into the on-and-off conflict, Tehran has concluded that the surest route to relief runs not through the battlefield but through the voting booths of Tel Aviv and Washington – hoping, in effect, that voters will do what its missiles could not.
Publicly, Iranian officials show contempt for the elections.
Asked about the Israeli election , Esmail Baghaei, the foreign ministry spokesman, likened it to the Cold War satire Dr Strangelove.
“I don’t think there’s really an election there,” he told reporters in Tehran on Monday. “It’s a competition between rival gangs over who can commit more evil – a contest over who can kill more.”
It made no difference, he added, “who ends up at the helm of a regime whose only achievement for our region has been killing and violence”.
Privately, however, the calculation is colder and more confident.
“For us it does not matter who wins or who loses any of the elections in America or Israel,” a third senior Iranian official told The Telegraph.
“Whoever wins in Israel , they will still be the enemy. And in America, it would be good to see voters, who are angry at their warmonger ruler, make a decision that would bring peace to the world.”
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, was pushing for renewed strikes on Iran in the run-up to the election, according to reports.
He frequently warned that Israel might face annihilation at the hands of Tehran if his time as prime minister ended.
But the Iranian official warned that any renewed assault would be met more broadly than before.
“In Tehran, we are not sitting and waiting for their election results, and we are in charge of the war,” he said.
“Ready to make meaningful peace, and ready for a harsh response – and our reaction will not be limited only to American assets, like the previous time.”
In Israel, the thing Tehran wants most is paralysis.
A government consumed by coalition haggling and domestic reckoning is a distracted one, buying Iran time to rebuild the missile and air defence stocks damaged by this year’s strikes.
A deadlocked result could leave a caretaker government with no mandate for a major new offensive, or force a repeat election that freezes decisions for months.
Dr Steven Wagner, a senior lecturer in international security at Brunel University of London, said Iran had good reason to watch and wait rather than act.
“I would expect Iran has been hoping for Netanyahu to lose, and for the criminal proceedings against him to disqualify him from future office,” he said.
“We won’t know what will happen in Israel for a few days, as forming a government takes time, and Bibi is very likely to use every second of it and attempt to stall.”
Mr Netanyahu’s opponents, Mr Wagner said, faced their own dilemmas, “whether to go back on promises and form a coalition with Arab parties,” and whether Gadi Eisenkot , the prime minister’s leading rival, would accept “a path to end the war in Gaza, or a crackdown on settler violence”.
He added: “From Iran’s point of view, there is plenty of time to wait and see what happens, to continue to consolidate what hasn’t been destroyed and to bolster defences where they need to.
“I would not expect any major action from Iran under the circumstances, as it would disturb their very good chances for favourable outcomes in both cases.”
Iranian officials have followed the mechanics of the Israeli elections closely. As it stands, neither the pro-Netanyahu or anti-Netanyahu bloc has enough seats to form a majority.
With nearly 86 per cent of votes tallied on Wednesday, Israel’s three main broadcasters projected Netanyahu’s bloc of Right-wing, far-Right and ultra-Orthodox parties would win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
Parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Mr Eisenkot little realistic path to power without their broad backing – which many Jewish political leaders reject.
Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the national security and foreign policy committee in the Iranian parliament, said the Arab parties were pursuing two goals: blocking a victory for Mr Netanyahu and winning enough seats to shape the formation of the next government.
“Although the Arab parties do not by themselves have the seats to form a government, in a situation where none of the rival camps can secure a majority, even a limited number of seats can prove decisive,” he said.
Netanyahu will not ally with them, Mr Maleki said, and Mr Eisenkot faces his own constraints, since a formal pact with Arab parties “could cause part of his voter base to waver”.
If no deal is reached, he warned, “the likelihood of continued political deadlock rises” and with it the chance of a fresh election “that could place greater political and administrative pressure on the regime in the middle of a war”.
It is Washington, however, where Iranian optimism runs highest.
The midterm elections on Nov 3 will decide control of the House and a third of the Senate. Tehran is betting they will clip Donald Trump’s wings and return Democrats to Congress, restraining what one official called the US president’s “madness”.
Dr Wagner said: “Iran will be looking at the US midterms for signals that Congress might restrain the White House’s spending on the war and on Israel.”
Amir Ali Abolfath, an Iranian analyst of American affairs, laid out why Tehran has hopes – and why it should temper them.
Three indicators, he said, point the same way – the tradition that a ruling party loses ground in its first midterm, which “works against the Republicans”; polling that gives Democrats the better chance in the House, and betting markets that put their odds of taking the House at “around 75 to 80 per cent”.
The Senate race “is a harder contest” Mr Abolfath said, with the markets offering the Democrats a 60 per cent chance of victory. But Republicans “have thrown everything into holding the Senate”, and a hostile Congress would not by itself halt the war.
“A Congress not aligned with the president can create obstacles and headaches,” he said, “but one should not imagine that a Democratic victory alone would prevent war, because they do not fully hold that power, and the US president, as commander-in-chief, has considerable authority to launch or resume an attack.”
Mr Abolfath warned that the vote could accelerate, rather than delay, a new strike on Iran.
The White House might calculate that it could “end the war in three or four days”, and declare on the eve of the election that it had forced Iran to surrender, handing the Republicans a victory, he said.

articles.title_orig: Taipei mayor gets angry reception at Pride after gay bar raid
articles.title_zh: Taipei mayor gets angry reception at Pride after gay bar raid
articles.content_orig:
The rounding up of customers at a gay bar weeks before Saturday’s Pride festival has some questioning the island’s progressive image
J osh was having a drink at Commander D, a popular gay bar in Taipei, on a Saturday afternoon when several police officers suddenly burst in. “Squat down and don’t move,” they shouted. Bewildered, he looked around to see the bar owner being handcuffed and forced to his knees.
The 28-year-old was among 51 customers to be rounded up and taken away for questioning over suspected breaches of public decency rules.
“I didn’t expect something like this to still happen these days. It definitely made me feel a lot less safe,” says Josh, a gay man from Taiwan whose name has been changed due to the sensitivity of the incident. The police operation was criticised by rights groups as heavy-handed, and has unsettled LGBTQ+ communities in Taiwan.
On Saturday the island hosts one of the region’s largest Pride parades , and some say the police operation is emblematic of a persistent, wider stigma that risks jeopardising its global image as a LGBTQ -friendly destination.
The raid took place on 3 October at a bar that is billed as Taipei’s first and only BDSM-themed bar and features in several international travel guides. Commander D has operated for more than a decade in the Ximending area – a hub for LGBTQ+ tourists where gay bars and sex shops can be easily spotted.
The bar’s owner was arrested and referred to prosecutors on suspicion of profiting from facilitating sexual or indecent acts, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.
In the days after the raid, the police department said that it had received 13 complaints this year alleging public decency violations at the bar.
In an interview with Taiwanese media on 7 October, the bar owner accused the police of using excessive force and said that any intimate encounters between customers were a matter of personal choice. He has not yet been formally charged with any offences. His lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing investigation.
Videos posted on social media showed the police mocking a disabled customer and preventing some people from putting their clothes back on. Some had taken their shirts off because it was a warm day. Police said they had reviewed 41 body cam recordings and acknowledged inappropriate language had been used by its officers.
“There was an element of sexual humiliation,” says Victoria Hsu, a human rights lawyer specialising in LGBTQ+ rights. As police refused to let the patrons get dressed, “they weren’t allowed to go to the police station with dignity”.
The police department said their actions were intended to bring the scene under control and the court-authorised search had not targeted any particular group or sexual orientation. Yet after a strong public backlash, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an apologised and six police officers were disciplined for inappropriate remarks and failing to supervise their juniors properly. Rights groups are calling for an independent investigation.
Wanhua police division said rights groups filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors on 7 October. “The matter has entered the judicial process, and we await the outcome of the investigation and any subsequent court proceedings.”
Midnight Poonkasetwattana, executive director of the Bangkok-based LGBTQ+ advocacy network APCOM, told Taiwan’s Central news agency that the raid “could undermine the gay-friendly image Taiwan has built”.
Hung Yan-an, a gay man living in Taipei, says he received messages from overseas friends about the incident. “A gay friend of mine in Spain has been asking me: ‘Is everything OK? If I visit, will it be safe to hold hands with my partner in the street?’”
The episode stands in stark contrast to a recent survey that found public support for gay marriage has increased from 42% to 54% since Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, the first place in Asia to do so.
“But inclusion is not only about marriage equality, Pride or international recognition. It is also about how public institutions treat LGBTQI+ people when exercising state power,” Poonkasetwattana said in a formal letter of protest to Taiwan’s representative in Thailand over the decision to raid Commander D.
Local campaigners say the raid exposes a persistent stigma around queer venues, as well as “homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power that have long been embedded in the police system”.
A spokesperson for the Wanhua police division did not directly address the allegations of longstanding institutional homophobia but said it “fully respects social and cultural diversity and people’s rights” and would continue to combat crime and enforce the law to maintain public order.
Other gay venues have also faced scrutiny. In April, a gay bathhouse in the central city of Taichung closed after a police raid over suspected public-decency offences and subsequent inspections. In a Facebook statement announcing the closure, its owner accused police of discriminatory treatment. A gay gym in Taipei, which closed in 2021, had reportedly been inspected 186 times over three years.
“Some police officers assume that gay people are more likely to have drugs on them,” lawyer Hsu says. “I’ve had quite a few LGBTQ+ people come to me for legal advice, for example, some of them were subjected to improper police searches.”
For Chien Shih-han, a Taiwanese drag queen who performs as Hannah, discrimination is not always easy to identify. He recalls gay venues facing repeated noise complaints and a pre-booked taxi driving away after the driver saw a friend in drag.
“It could all come down to this subtle sense of discomfort or anxiety towards sexual minorities,” Chien says.
In his view, gay venues such as Commander D have offered a refuge to people who do not fit the mainstream, even within the LGBTQ+ community. “It was a kind of safety net,” Chien says. “Now it feels as though someone is setting fire to that net.”
Weeks later, Josh says he still feels “a little scared” when thinking back to the raid, but that it would not stop him taking to the streets for Taiwan Pride.
“I want to express my anger at being taken to the police station that day,” he says, “I want to go with the message that we’re not strange, we’re not freaks.”

Three American servicemembers were killed in a July 17 Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in the Jordanian desert. Satellite imagery shows the nighttime attack damaged at least 19 buildings where troops sleep.
It was one of the deadliest nights of the war for U.S. forces. But it wasn’t the only attack targeting American troops where they live and sleep. That same week, Iran hit multiple housing units at other U.S. military installations across the region.
The July strikes marked an alarming shift in Iran’s tactics and revealed an improvement in the regime’s ability to sequence attacks and hit targets with precision. Iran was taking more direct aim at the buildings that house American troops, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis of satellite data, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials.
The Journal’s analysis offers the most comprehensive public accounting of the war’s damage to American facilities to date.

articles.title_orig: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure
articles.title_zh: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over.
Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. The S&P 500 followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%.
"After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the " Mad Money " host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings."
"My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher."
With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.
Apple reports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said.
Cramer also expects encouraging results from Palantir when it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software.
The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them."
On the earnings front, Advanced Micro Devices reports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector following Intel's disappointing results . Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel.
Drugmakers Pfizer and Amgen also report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks.
CVS Health reports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said.
McDonald's earnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees.
Kimberly-Clark reports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger with Kenvue . The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said.
The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields.
The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners.

articles.title_orig: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
articles.title_zh: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
articles.content_orig:

“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”
I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh !), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.
When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.
As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases . I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.
As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.
There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”
As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)
I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.
Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.
Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.
This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)
In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.
For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.
Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.
I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.
However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.
This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.
It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.
Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.
There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.
Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID .)
Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.
Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.
For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

articles.title_orig: Binance, crypto and hacks: What to know about keeping coin safe as cyber criminals advance
articles.title_zh: Binance, crypto and hacks: What to know about keeping coin safe as cyber criminals advance
articles.content_orig:
For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression.
Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.
In a security update on Saturday, the exchange said it had replenished 90% of stolen assets and was committed to covering the remaining 10%. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea , but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack.
Understanding how crypto is protected online and what mechanisms exist to serve a role similar to insurance is increasingly important as more Americans invest in cryptocurrency.
Roughly one in five U.S. adults say they have invested in, traded, or used crypto , according to Pew Research Center, a figure that is even higher among upper income households (27%). The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy.
While Binance was making good on its pledge in the aftermath of the hack to cover all losses with its SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users) and other company's funds — and that there's no evidence of a wallet private-key leak in this incident — Nikolas Behar, a cybersecurity expert and professor at the University of San Diego, said crypto investors need to understand when using crypto platforms that a pledge is just a pledge "until there's an actual payout."
If something happens to your crypto, most consumers are left to navigate a patchwork of options that vary from exchange to exchange and are often very ambiguous. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong.
Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance."
Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said.
Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so."
"Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said.
"Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone.
Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack.
"When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute.
Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach.
"The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. But he added that the details of this hack point to a larger problem.
"Binance says no keys were leaked. The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one.
"On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death.
"Moving savings off an exchange trades one kind of risk for another. It does not remove risk," Tanguma said.
Sarah Downey, executive vice president and global blockchain and digital assets advisory leader at Lockton, an insurance brokerage, said other factors also come into play in determining whether you can get your crypto back, including how quickly the theft is discovered, where the funds were moved, whether the exchange or wallet provider has insurance that covers the event, and whether it holds enough reserves to repay customers.
"Some companies have set up FDIC-like insurance or other backstops, but whether these pay out depends heavily on the facts of each case. Even without insurance, many exchanges try to repay customers from their own reserves to protect both their customers and their own reputation," Downey said.
Crypto exchange reimbursements have followed other security compromises, such as after rogue overseas support agents were bribed to help scam Coinbase customers in May 2025. Bitget, another major exchange, had to tap an in-house fund to reimburse customers after a $388 million hack in September. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said its User Protection Fund, which held more than $464 million, covered the loss. "The Protection Fund was created for moments like this and absorbed the financial impact of the incident," Chen said in a post on X at the time.
By comparison, Binance's emergency reserve, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, is estimated at roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, and excluding the funds that were frozen, this represented about one-third of the loss. The company said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds and already held more than $5 billion in corresponding token assets.
Downey said the steps to take if your crypto is hacked depend on whether investors self-custody or use a third party, such as a regulated exchange.
"If they use a third party, they should check that most funds are stored offline or protected with multi-party computation. An investor's own funds should also be stored separately from the exchange's own funds," Downey said, adding that customers should also understand how the custodian authorizes transactions and governs storage.
Ryan Reck, founder and principal of Reck Advisory, an independent cybersecurity advisory firm, points to the lack of oversight of crypto.
"Crypto has no undo button. Once a transfer confirms, there's no chargeback and no one who can reverse it," Reck said. In some cases, stolen funds can be frozen by an exchange that receives them, or by a stablecoin issuer at a specific blockchain address, but tracing the money and getting it back are two different things.

articles.title_orig: Starmer tells Dublin event Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence
articles.title_zh: Starmer tells Dublin event Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence
articles.content_orig:
Sir Keir Starmer has said Europe should build a common security framework, warning the change in its defence relationship with the US is permanent rather than "an aberration of the Trump presidency".
The former prime minister was speaking at a British Irish Chamber of Commerce (BICC) dinner in Dublin on Friday evening.
Sir Keir said a "common security framework" for Europe was needed as much as a common market, with the UK at its centre.
He warned that "things will not go back to the way they were," adding that the US had made clear it will no longer "bankroll" its European allies.
Press Association reported that he told the crowd in Dublin City Hall his comments did not mean "the US relationship is no longer important".
Rather he said the UK-USA military, security and intelligence alliance was "far too strong for that".
But he said Europe must be enabled to "take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security".
"Europe has twice been caught asleep – failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events," he said.
"First when Russia's attack on Ukraine exposed long-standing European weaknesses on defence and security; and second when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up," he added.
He added: "I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.
Sir Keir was at the dinner to be awarded an honorary life membership from the BICC.
Sir Keir said increased defence spending was part of the picture, but that the challenge "goes far beyond that."
"We need to build up pan-European co-operation and co-ordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market," he said.
"The EU is changing to respond to that," he said, warning that it "cannot be the EU alone when Europe's periphery is core to its defence."
In July Sir Keir said he would "keep in touch" with President Trump after his time as prime minister ended.
The pair developed a positive relationship in their opening months of working together, which Sir Keir's team highlighted at the time as one of the biggest successes of his premiership.
But Trump later mocked Sir Keir as being "no Winston Churchill" in a row over the refusal to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran.
Sir Keir, asked whether Trump had wished him well as he prepared to leave Downing Street, said: "Yes he did, and we're going to stay in touch."

articles.title_orig: Florida woman, 75, lost $25K in a fake sweepstakes — deputies say a New York flight attendant flew in and got onto her Apple Card
articles.title_zh: Florida woman, 75, lost $25K in a fake sweepstakes — deputies say a New York flight attendant flew in and got onto her Apple Card
articles.content_orig:
A 75-year-old Florida woman thought she had won a sweepstakes. Instead, investigators say, she lost more than $25,000 in a scheme that began after a caller posing as a Publishers Clearing House representative convinced her to pay to collect her prize.
But the alleged scam didn’t stop at cash and gift cards. Investigators say a 24-year-old New York flight attendant flew to Florida, made her way to the woman’s home and gained access to her Apple Card account. She allegedly spent thousands using a card linked to the victim’s account.

Destiny Blake of Brooklyn was arrested Oct. 23 at Miami International Airport after an international flight, according to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office . She now faces several felony charges, including organizing a scheme to defraud over $20,000 from a victim 65 or older, fraudulent use of personal identification information of a person 60 or older and grand theft over $20,000. She has since been released on a $30,000 bond.
It started with a phone call in November 2025. The voice on the other end told the 75-year-old victim that she had won a prize and needed to mail a $500 gift card to Blake at a Brooklyn address to collect her “winnings,” according to the sheriff’s office.
Around the same time as the initial call, the victim was locked out of her email account after its password was changed and the account switched to a lookalike address, investigators said.
Between Nov. 15 and Nov. 19, 2025, the woman withdrew more than $14,000 from her bank. Blake allegedly received $14,220 through cash payments and Zelle transfers.
Then, on Nov. 18, Blake used her American Airlines employee travel benefits to fly standby from New York to Daytona Beach, then took an Uber to a hotel in Palm Coast. The following morning, an Uber dropped her at the victim’s home. She left about 15 minutes later.
Investigators say Blake had become an authorized user on the woman’s Apple Card account. A family member later found a handwritten note at the home telling the victim to contact the card issuer and say Blake was her granddaughter and had permission to use the card.
From Nov. 16 to Dec. 11, investigators identified 88 transactions totaling $10,590.30. Purchases included Apple products, an eBay order delivered to Blake’s Brooklyn home, T-Mobile and Ugg purchases, salon visits and Uber rides. In total, the woman’s losses were estimated at $25,310.

An authorized user gets their own card, but the account still belongs to the primary cardholder. That means purchases made by anyone on the account show up on the same bill — and the primary cardholder is generally responsible for paying it. Basically, you can hand someone a card without handing over responsibility for the charges.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing. For example, parents might add a teenager to help them learn how credit works or someone might give a partner or family member a card for everyday expenses. The arrangement depends on the primary cardholder being comfortable with how that person will use it.
In this case, investigators say Blake allegedly went much further, using the victim’s Apple Card to make thousands of dollars in purchases after gaining access to the account.
The woman was also allegedly given instructions on what to tell the card issuer about Blake’s relationship to her. If someone asks you to add them to your account as part of a supposed prize claim, that’s a good reason to stop and call your card issuer directly. Use the number on the back of your card or the issuer’s official website rather than the number provided by the caller.
The Federal Trade Commission also warns that legitimate sweepstakes don’t charge winners to collect a prize. If someone asks for a gift card, cash, a wire transfer or your financial information, you can be pretty confident that the prize isn’t what they say it is. In this case, the woman was asked to send a $500 gift card before the alleged scam took an even more costly turn.

articles.title_orig: AI Enthusiasm Is Collapsing and Tech Earnings Just Made It Worse
articles.title_zh: AI Enthusiasm Is Collapsing and Tech Earnings Just Made It Worse
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
And you thought this week has been painful for the tech trade.
If history is any guide, the pain for tech may only be just beginning!
The S&P 500 tech sector has seen six pullbacks of 10% or more since 2023, points out Truist chief markets strategist officer (chart below), including the current one. But four of the six plunges have ranged from 14% to 27%.
"The story is no longer simply about the strength of AI demand. Wall Street is increasingly demanding evidence that heavy investment will translate into durable profits and cash flow," Lerner says.
That's putting it lightly.
The AI trade took a serious beating Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech as it spends aggressively on AI. The news on the cash front worsened as the weak went along.
Google showed negative free cash flow in the third quarter when it reported mid-week. That was followed by another free cash flow negative call out when Amazon reported Thursday evening.
A week ago, Meta posted negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012.
None of these top tech names suggested their AI spending would be slowing down, quite the contrary.
The Nasdaq 100 went onto tank 3.4% while the broader S&P 500 fell 1.8%.
The S&P 500's tech sector tumbled more than 4.2%.
"The disruption caused by AI is on full display during tech earnings and the uncertainty around which names and sectors will be the disruptors vs the disrupted," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives said. "This is not the time to panic and sell all the tech winners and head into the bunker…as painful as this week is the underlying signs from enterprise AI buildouts are actually more validated than a week ago…given what we heard front and center from the hyperscalers combined with last week's Meta and SpaceX ( SPCX ) numbers. That said, tech players raising money via the bond market, equity offerings, ATMs, etc. has put further pressure on the sector and adding to the overhang seen this week."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: Trump promised to slash energy costs — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
articles.title_zh: Trump promised to slash energy costs — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office.
"My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign.
"Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon."
But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
"Prices have never been this high this late in the year," De Haan said.
Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year. The price of diesel, critical to transportation and agriculture, has surged about 70% over the past year, to $6.32 a gallon.
During the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, the year that Russia invaded Ukraine and triggered an energy crisis, retail gas prices stood at $3.80, according to AAA data.
"Trump got in his own way," De Haan said. "Back in December, we predicted that 2026 was going to be the cheapest year for gas since 2020. That required no effort. And obviously, it hasn't gone that way."
Fuel prices have spiked since Trump decided to attack Iran in a joint attack with Israel on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with a wave of strikes on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, severely depressing oil flows through the vital shipping route.
Trump told voters at a rally in Michigan last Sunday that rising fuel prices are a "small price to pay" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The White House said gas prices when adjusted for inflation have been higher around previous election days.
Exports through Hormuz have rebounded since the summer as the U.S. military helped ships through the strait. But the Middle East disruption has been compounded by Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi Arabian refineries, and Ukraine's strikes on refineries in Russia. Trump had promised to end that war in the first week of his second term, but the conflict is stuck in an intractable stalemate.
"Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth," ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday after the nation's largest oil company posted huge profits thanks to the disruptions.
Airlines have hiked their fares to cover high costs from jet fuel, their biggest expense other than labor, hurting the fight to contain inflation.
Trump came under political pressure from Republicans to take action on fuel prices ahead of Tuesday's election. The cost of diesel is hurting big farm states like Iowa that have overwhelmingly backed Trump in his presidential campaigns. The senate race in the Hawkeye State has become competitive.
Trump briefly contemplated a diesel export ban as Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) lobbied to help the state's farmers. The president decided against it because it might also have raised gasoline prices.
Instead, Trump issued an executive order to allow truckers to use tax-exempt, offroad diesel on U.S. highways, and announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Trump later struck a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to export about 6 million barrels of diesel into the global market through November.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and even some Republican senators slammed the agreement as rewarding Russian aggression. Energy analysts said the diesel volumes in the Russia deal are small compared to global demand and won't have a meaningful impact on prices.
More recently, crude oil prices have rallied ahead of the election. Trump has said he will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterms. But the market is pricing in the risk of another round of fighting after voting ends on Tuesday. International Brent crude oil prices are up more than 13% in October and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 15%.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," De Haan said, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."

articles.title_orig: Iran buying time in nuclear talks as US prepares for possible strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran buying time in nuclear talks as US prepares for possible strikes
articles.content_orig:
Israel's defense establishment is maintaining ambiguity regarding preparations for a possible escalation with Iran, as the White House gives the Iranian regime another opportunity to return to negotiations, according to Israeli defense assessments on Friday.
Defense officials assess that the Iranians, who are facing an economic crisis that is worsening from week to week, will not sign an agreement requiring them to completely abandon their nuclear program, and certainly will not agree to stop producing ballistic missiles that now also threaten Europe. Accordingly, the assessment is that Iran is merely attempting to buy time. Iran has reportedly been deliberately prolonging negotiations ahead of the US midterm elections.
Meanwhile, Iranian security agencies have succeeded in suppressing the first signs of resistance in the streets and preventing renewed protest movements from organizing.
Defense officials further assess that despite preparations by the US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) for a possible strike on Iran, the White House will not order an operation against the Iranian regime before the US midterm elections unless it detects preparations for a surprise attack. The US and Israel have also reportedly drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms .
It is worth noting that more than 3,000 American troops are currently stationed in Israel, and no sharp increase was recorded in the number of US military aircraft redirected to the country during the previous week. This contrasts with the unprecedented deployment of US military refueling aircraft that filled the runways at Ben-Gurion Airport and Ramon Airport, alongside a significant presence at Israeli Air Force bases.
Against this backdrop, Israel's defense establishment assesses that immediately after the US midterm elections, the White House will renew pressure on Jerusalem to advance the establishment of a terrorism-free Palestinian city on the ruins of Rafah, funded by the United Arab Emirates.
According to a defense source, there is approval in principle to establish a "bubble" within Palestinian territory that is currently under a high degree of IDF operational control.
IDF troops are still operating in the designated area in the southern Gaza Strip, searching for unexploded ordnance, explosive devices, and infrastructure above and below ground.
At least according to the original plan, the first phase is intended to accommodate tens of thousands of Palestinians.
Senior defense officials oppose any progress toward rebuilding the Gaza Strip without first disarming Hamas and demilitarizing the territory, including transferring governing authority from Hamas to a third party. US officials and representatives of the Board of Peace have been preparing to identify locations for Hamas weapons handovers under the US-backed plan.
Senior Southern Command officials told Walla during the week that Hamas has no intention of disarming and has backed away from the proposal to surrender its weapons and place them in storage facilities inside the Gaza Strip.
Accordingly, Southern Command officials assess that regardless of which government is formed, the IDF is preparing for a ground maneuver aimed at capturing Gaza City and dismantling the terrorist infrastructure within it.
In addition, IDF troops in Hebron are preparing to demolish the homes of the terrorists who carried out the attack in the city the previous week, in which two active-duty soldiers were killed. The deadly Hebron terrorist attack prompted extensive IDF operations in the area. The home demolitions are expected to take place on Saturday.
For this reason, a decision was made not to reduce troop levels until the mission is completed.

articles.title_orig: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.title_zh: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.content_orig:
An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.
The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
"The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang.
"We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology.
As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure.
Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed.
"Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

articles.title_orig: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed
articles.title_zh: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.
Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.
"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jared Beck, head of Rivian's additive manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."
Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.
Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.
Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.
Beck said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.
"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Beck said.
The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.
"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Beck said.
Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.
There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors , which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.
Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.
"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."
Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.
Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.
Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.
Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.
"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.
Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.
GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.
The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.
Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.
"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

articles.title_orig: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
articles.title_zh: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
articles.content_orig:
It's a mega-recycling effort: A crew of 60 men use blow torches and winches to break down a ship that had carried liquid natural gas. Tons of metal parts will be harvested to resell overseas. This photo by George Steinmetz, from the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh, is the overall winner in the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards contest. George Steinmetz hide caption
It looks like a spacecraft that settled gently onto a golden beach.
Off the coast of Bangladesh, an enormous vessel lies stranded on the mudflats, its steel hull partially dismantled as workers mill around it. This unusual aerial view of a tanker, specially designed to transport liquified natural gas used for cooking, electricity and transport, won photographer George Steinmetz the top prize — overall winner of the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards.
Each year, the Siena Drone Photo Awards highlight bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground. Here, we've selected some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs, focusing on the countries of the Global South.
In an interview with NPR, Steinmetz says he's been long fascinated by Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe, nearing the end of their working lives, are dismantled and their materials recovered for reuse. The photograph is titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal." Steinmetz sent up his drone north of Chattogram (Chittagong), along this 13-mile coastal strip, offering a stark glimpse into what this industry is like.
He was exploring the relationship between human populations and the environment for a book project and saw the industry as an extraordinary example of recycling on a vast scale.
Photographing it proved surprisingly difficult. The ship breaking industry has faced criticism from environmental organizations, human rights groups, labor unions and non-governmental organizations for its unchecked pollution, the leeching of chemicals into the sea and dangerous working conditions . Shipyard owners are wary of journalists and photographers. Local photographers initially warned Steinmetz that securing access might be nearly impossible.
Undeterred, he surveyed and photographed the entire coastline north of Chattogram with his drone, searching for a vessel that would make an especially striking photograph. He eventually settled on the liquid natural gas tanker. "The trick for me was to find the right ship, that was in a really interesting state of disassembly. And these tankers are very unusual boats. It just looked weird, like some kind of a spaceship. It takes workers a long time to break it down. And then they have to wait for the tide to be right so they can pull the pieces ashore. They have big winches and boats that they use to get the stuff ashore."
He was able to convince the owner of the tanker to allow him to photograph it. The timing of the drone photo was crucial. Steinmetz wanted to capture the vessel at low tide, when the surrounding mudflats were exposed and workers could be seen moving around its enormous hull. Their tiny figures would look like ants, giving viewers a sense of the ship's mammoth scale. He spent several days photographing the vessel, returning as the tides shifted and the workers continued to take the ship apart for scrap metal.
After graduating from Stanford with a degree in geophysics in 1979, Steinmetz had first dreamed of photographing landscapes from above while hitchhiking across Africa, often traveling on the roofs of trucks.
In 1996, National Geographic agreed to finance an aerial photography project around the Sahara, for which Steinmetz learned to fly a motorized paraglider. "It was like being in a flying lawn chair or [sitting on] the front of a spoon," he says. Drones have now completely transformed aerial photography, allowing photographers to capture the world from perspectives that were once difficult, expensive or impossible to achieve, Steinmetz says.
Today, armed with a drone rather than a paraglider, he continues to explore how a view from the sky can reveal stories that remain invisible from the ground.
Fields of handwoven carpets transform into a visual tapestry, laid out under the sun to dry. The weeks, even months, of exposure to intense sunlight gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. F. Dilek Yurdakul hide caption
Why would anyone spread hundreds of beautiful carpets across open fields, leaving them exposed to a blazing Mediterranean sun for weeks or even months?
In southern Türkiye, this is part of a traditional process that gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. Under the intense sunlight, the vibrant reds, blues and other hues gradually mellow into glowing, muted tones.
For Ankara-based documentary photographer and lawyer Dilek Yurdakul, the drone was not simply a technical choice. It was an essential storytelling tool. "I wanted to create an image that first attracts the viewer through its beauty but then invites them to look deeper, to discover the people, traditions and cultural memory behind it," she says. The photograph won first place in the contest's People section.
Yurdakul traveled six hours in blistering heat from Ankara to the Döşemealtı district of Antalya to capture this spectacle. "The first sight was astonishing. The fields were far larger than I had imagined. Thousands of carpets and kilims in different colors, sizes and patterns stretched across an enormous landscape," she says. From above, the carpets resemble a giant patchwork quilt, almost as if melded together, but her photograph captures the shadows between these slices of color.
The aerial perspective allowed her to bring together several layers of the story in a single frame, she says: the artistic richness of Anatolian craftsmanship, the scale of the landscape and the human labor that connects them.
"For me, this was a visual metaphor for the invisibility of labor. In many societies, the people whose work sustains everyday life remain largely unseen and unrecognized."
The Tumpak Sewu waterfall in Indonesia cascades from the cliffs. The drone's eye view shows Senaru Volcano rising in the distance, sending smoke into the sky. Colas Decloitre hide caption
In this photo, highly commended in the Nature category, an imposing horseshoe-shaped waterfall spills over the cliffs of East Java, Indonesia, at sunrise . Boston-based, French-British drone photographer Colas Decloitre had hoped to capture the interesting shape of the waterfall with Mount Semeru rising behind it. What he hadn't anticipated was catching the active volcano behind the waterfall, glowing red and writhed with ash, in the middle of an eruption.
"The only way to get the right alignment of the waterfall and the volcano is with a drone, as you can only be on the side of the waterfall yourself," he says. Using his drone, he could position the waterfall against the volcano, revealing an intriguing landscape that could only be viewed from the air.
A small scoria cone glows crimson amid the volcanic deserts of the Argentine Puna. Surrounded by ancient lava flows, ash deposits and wind-sculpted terrain, it stands as a final ember in a landscape forged by fire. Isabella Tabacchi hide caption
It looks like the glowing eye of a fiery monster.
It's actually a volcanic cone, the pile of rock, ash and hardened lava that builds up around the mouth of the volcano over time.
The Last Ember , by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi , is an example of how a drone photo has the power to transform landscapes into a dream-like quality. It was a commended entry in the Nature category.
The photo was taken in the Argentine Puna, a vast, remote, high-altitude plateau in the Andes of northwestern Argentina: a landscape of volcanoes, ancient lava fields, salt flats and desert mountains. The cone's reddish color comes from iron-bearing minerals in the volcanic rock, while the s

articles.title_orig: Iran court sentences 21-year-old protester to death
articles.title_zh: Iran court sentences 21-year-old protester to death
articles.content_orig:
A court in Iran has sentenced 21-year-old protester Omran Amani to death on a charge of "moharebeh," or "waging war against God," according to information obtained by Iran International.
Amani was sentenced on October 24 by Branch 26 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Iman Afshari.
Amani was arrested on February 11, following Iran's nationwide December-January protests, when Basij and intelligence officers raided his shared home in Tehran and detained him alongside two friends, Alireza Dolati and Mohammad Khalizadeh, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.
The three men worked as motorcycle couriers for SnappBox, an Iranian delivery service, the source said.
According to the source, security personnel severely beat the men during their arrest, and Amani was subsequently held in solitary confinement for two months.
The source said Amani's right shoulder was broken during torture aimed at extracting a forced confession at Tehran's Evin Prison and that he had not received adequate medical treatment for the injury.
His case also includes accusations of conspiracy against national security and conducting operational or intelligence activities on behalf of Israel or other hostile governments or groups.
After the US-Iran war began on February 28, Amani was transferred from Evin Prison to Greater Tehran Prison, where he remains held in Ward 6, according to the source.
UN warns of executions and mass trials
The sentence comes amid growing international scrutiny of Iran's treatment of protesters arrested during nationwide demonstrations earlier this year.
UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran Mai Sato told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that Iranian authorities had executed at least 34 people in connection with the January protests and conducted mass trials resulting in death sentences.
She cited one case in which 34 defendants were tried in five days, with 12 sentenced to death and seven subsequently executed.
Sato said the proceedings failed to establish individual criminal responsibility and warned that thousands of detainees had been held on national security charges, often without access to their families or lawyers.
"The result is that there is no lawful way left to dissent," she said.
The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission concluded that the suppression of the January protests amounted to crimes against humanity, a finding Sato supported.
The book, launched in London on October 21, was written inside prison “on scraps of newspaper and tissue paper and whatever else she could find,” according to Payam Akhavan, the international human rights lawyer who hosted the event.
The fragments were later smuggled out of Iran and assembled by Azita Mottahedeh, a scholar, and writer Bahiyyih Nakhjavani., the book’s translators
Sabet trained as a teacher and was a member of the “Yaran,” or “Friends” of Iran, a group tasked, with the government's knowledge, with caring for the Baha’i community’s basic needs.
More than 200 Baha’is were executed after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and the community continues to face widespread discrimination and persecution.
After Sabet’s arrest in 2008, the other six members of the Yaran were also detained. All seven were jailed for a decade on charges including conspiring against national security. Their former lawyer, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi, has said no evidence was presented to substantiate the charges.
Released in 2017, Sabet was arrested again in 2022 and sentenced to another decade in prison alongside fellow former Yaran member Fariba Kamalabadi. She is currently on medical furlough but could be recalled to prison at any time.
The book offers an unflinching account of prison conditions. In solitary confinement, the stench is so “noxious” that Sabet tries to breathe through a slit in her door. Other prisoners’ faeces lie in piles in her cell, and cockroaches crawl across the floor.
Remembering hours of blindfolded questioning early in her detention, Sabet writes that “the hair rose on the back of my neck” each time her interrogator drew close.
But alongside the degradation and violence, the memoir describes Sabet’s efforts to preserve compassion for those around her, including fellow prisoners and even her jailers.
At the London launch, two former cellmates and another former prisoner spoke about Sabet’s influence on their lives.
Roxana Saberi, a journalist imprisoned in Evin in 2009, recalled being “dumbfounded” when Sabet and Kamalabadi told her they were “trying to turn their experiences [in prison] into an opportunity.”
As Sabet showed “kindness and compassion to everyone, from her fellow cellmates to her captors,” Saberi came to believe that such an approach could help lay the foundations for “democracy, freedom and understanding” in Iran.
One episode in the memoir captures that compassion. When an “emaciated” crack addict, with “a head like a prop for an anatomy class … eyes set back in deep rings of darkness,” reaches toward Sabet from a lower bunk, she climbs down to hold the woman’s hand.
Although Sabet has only just secured a bed in an overcrowded ward, she also holds the woman’s wounded, “festering” feet, describing how her heart breaks and fills with love.
Sabet does not conceal her own suffering. After a brutal interrogation in which she endures insults and blows from six “sweating, stinking” men, she recalls how “desperate” she had been for “fresh air.”
Iqan Shahidi, an Iranian Baha’i imprisoned between 2012 and 2017, described Sabet as “like a light in the darkness for me.”
Now an academic in the United Kingdom, Shahidi said he had studied at the informal Baha’i university where Sabet taught before her imprisonment.
The institution illustrated how Baha’is responded to persecution, he said. Rather than resorting to political confrontation or violence, “instead they built something,” providing education to young Baha’is barred from public universities.
“Mahvash kept everybody so hopeful through very simple things in life,” said Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, the Iranian-British former prisoner who spent six years in detention.
Every year in prison, Zaghari-Ratcliffe recalled, Sabet invited the entire ward to a Nowruz feast. Tables were pushed together, and Sabet supervised the careful slicing of potatoes for traditional Persian dishes.
She continued paying for the annual celebration even after her release, sending money to jailed activist and future Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi.
For Zaghari-Ratcliffe, the gatherings represented something larger than a shared meal.
Iran’s political prisoners, drawn from different ethnic and religious communities and political backgrounds, were forced to live together for years despite their differences.
Sabet, she said, would “make sure that we [were] all part of the same community.”
“We are against this oppression that has put us in this place … regardless of our differences, we are all one.”
That commitment extended even to prison staff.
Sabet recounts returning to a jail where she had previously been held and receiving a warm welcome from guards. One officer, who tells her that “all my life I have been a good Muslim,” confesses that he has come to hate religion and works for the government only to support his family.
Sabet tries to reassure him, expressing her belief that Iran has a better future and that its people will one day rebuild the country together.
The officer says he wishes he could believe her.
“So allow yourself to,” Sabet replies, “instead of wasting energy on your doubts!”
In the book’s final pages, Sabet recalls an unexpected encounter in prison with Jamaloddin Khanjani, the eldest member of the Yaran.
“The sheer wonder of what had happened felt like a recompense for all the beatings, a reward after all that solitude; it was like breathing fresh air in the suffocating corridors of Evin.”
